context.title: Running payroll in five countries means five sets of deadlines, holidays and currencies
context.body: Rippling lets a company pay employees, EOR hires and contractors around the world from one system. But each country has its own approval window, bank holidays and funding currency, so 'when do I need to approve, and is the money there?' has a different answer for every entity. Admins piece it together from separate pay runs. A local holiday that moves a deadline is easy to miss until pay is late.
assumptions: I haven't used Rippling Global Payroll. My view comes from Rippling's product page, public reviews and the job post, so the product may already do some of this.
Rippling's footnote says eligible companies can approve 'up to 3 business days before payday'; I've used that rule in the example, but real cutoffs vary by country.
Brazil's 20 Nov national holiday is real; the company, people and amounts are fictional.
Visuals approximate Rippling's brand (deep plum bar, warm yellow accent) on a clean business layout. No Rippling logo.

goals.title: One view of every deadline
goals.body: Approve-by and payday for every country on one calendar.

goals.title: Explain moved dates
goals.body: When a local holiday shifts a deadline, say so before it's missed.

goals.title: Fund every currency on time
goals.body: Show what each currency needs, when, and from where.

jtbd: When I run payroll across countries, I want to see every approval deadline and funding need in one place, so nobody is paid late because of a date I didn't know had moved.

evidence.step: Approval windows depend on business days
evidence.finding: Rippling's footnote: eligible companies can approve payroll 'up to 3 business days before payday', excluding weekends and holidays, depending on market.
Rippling runs payroll for employees, EOR hires and contractors 'without switching tools', with localised tax and filing in supported markets.
Recent 2-star reviews mention pay transfers taking 'three working days' excluding holidays, support waits that 'stall urgent payroll questions', and gaps for international needs.
The team pays 'hundreds of thousands of employees over $50B annually' and wants to reimagine 'key workflows to support our scaling needs'.

source.label: YC: Rippling, Product Design Lead, Global Payroll

approaches: Keep one pay run per country
Put every country's deadlines on one calendar

ranges.title: Pay run list
ranges.summary: Today's common pattern: one pay run per country in a list.

ranges.title: Due-this-week banner
ranges.summary: A banner of approvals due, over the list.
cons: No reason when a date moves.

ranges.title: Global Pay Calendar
ranges.summary: Every country's approve-by and payday on one timeline, moved dates explained in place, and a funding plan per currency.
pros: One answer to 'what do I need to do this week?'.
Catches holiday shifts before they cost a payday.
cons: Needs reliable holiday and cutoff data per market.
Large companies need grouping by region.

decision.title: Global Pay Calendar: every country's deadline, in one view
decision.body: Range 3. A calendar of approve-by and payday for every entity, with local holidays marked; a side panel that explains why a deadline moved; and a funding plan that shows each currency's debit date and whether it's covered.
reasons: Admins think in weeks, not in separate pay runs.
A moved deadline is the error that's easiest to miss and costliest to fix.
Funding is part of being on time, so it belongs in the same view.
decision.tradeoff: The calendar is only as good as the cutoff and holiday data. I'd show the rule behind each date so admins can trust or question it.

depth.body: Built as a working Global Payroll screen for a fictional company with five entities. Three moments: a calendar where Brazil's approve-by is tomorrow because 20 Nov is a national holiday and the UK needs two National Insurance numbers; a panel explaining the moved date with the approve, debit and pay timeline; and a funding plan where BRL is short, with the option to convert from USD at approval. Panels ease in, and motion turns off for people who reduce it.

validation.method: I'd review late or off-cycle payrolls across countries with the payroll ops team, then test the calendar with five multi-country admins during a real cycle.
hypotheses: Fewer late approvals in countries with local holidays.
Admins spend less time checking each country's run.

metrics.name: Late approvals
metrics.definition: Pay runs approved after their cutoff, per 100 runs.

metrics.name: Funding shortfalls
metrics.definition: Debits that fail or need a top-up, per 100 runs.

metrics.name: Time to approve all
metrics.definition: Time from first to last approval across a company's countries.

nextSteps: Map cutoff and holiday rules per market with payroll ops.
Review late and off-cycle runs for patterns.
Design grouping for companies in 20+ countries.
